Given an instance 𝐼 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ) and a vertex 𝑢 ∈ 𝐶𝑈 (called the pivot vertex), let 𝑁 𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 ) = {𝑣 1, 𝑣 2, . . . , 𝑣𝑑𝑢 } denote the set of non-neighbors of 𝑢 in 𝐶𝑉 . Then, the maximum biclique in 𝐼 is equivalent to the maximum among the following 𝑑 𝑢 + 1 subinstances: (1) 𝐼 0 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 ∪ {𝑢}, 𝑆𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 \ {𝑢}, 𝑁𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 )); (2) 𝐼𝑖 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ∪ {𝑣𝑖 }, 𝑁 𝑣𝑖 (𝐶𝑈 ), 𝐶𝑉 \ {𝑣 1, . . . , 𝑣𝑖 }), where 𝑖 ∈ [1, 𝑑 𝑢 ]. Note that, in instance 𝐼 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ), Theorem 3.1 selects only one vertex from candidate sets as the pivot vertex to generate 𝑑 𝑢 + 1 subinstances, which is dramatically less than |𝐶𝑈 | + |𝐶𝑉 | subinstances generated by the traditional method. To obtain a better performance, we typically select the vertex with the fewest neighbors in 𝐺 (𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ) as the pivot vertex in practical implementations. Improved pivot-based techniques. Consider again the instance 𝐼 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ). After processing pivot vertex 𝑢 ∈ 𝐶𝑈 via subinstance 𝐼 0 , Theorem 3.1 will generate 𝑑 𝑢 subinstances by iteratively adding non-neighbors 𝑣 ∈ 𝑁 𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 ) to 𝑆𝑉 . However, if two vertices 𝑣 1, 𝑣 2 ∈ 𝑁 𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 ) satisfy 𝑁 𝑣1 (𝐶𝑈 ) ⊆ 𝑁 𝑣2 (𝐶𝑈 ), then any biclique in 𝐼 1 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ∪ {𝑣 1 }, 𝑁 𝑣1 (𝐶𝑈 ), 𝐶𝑉 ) is strictly non-maximum. This is because, for every biclique 𝐺 (𝐴𝑈 , 𝐵𝑉 ) in 𝐼 1 , 𝐺 (𝐴𝑈 , 𝐵𝑉 ∪ {𝑣 2 }) forms a larger biclique discoverable via 𝐼 2 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ∪ {𝑣 2 }, 𝑁 𝑣2 (𝐶𝑈 ), 𝐶𝑉 ), making 𝐼 1 redundant. Given an 𝐼 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ) and a pivot vertex 𝑢 ∈ 𝐶𝑈 , let 𝐷 = {𝑣 1, 𝑣 2, . . . , 𝑣𝑑 ′ } be the largest subset of 𝑁 𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 ) where 𝑁 𝑣𝑖 (𝐶𝑈 ) \ 𝑁 𝑣 𝑗 (𝐶𝑈 ) ≠ ∅ for all distinct 𝑣𝑖 , 𝑣 𝑗 ∈ 𝐷. Then, the maximum biclique in 𝐼 is equivalent to the maximum among the following |𝐷 | + 1 subinstances: (1) 𝐼 0 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 ∪ {𝑢}, 𝑆𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 \ {𝑢}, 𝑁𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 )); (2) 𝐼𝑖 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ∪ {𝑣𝑖 }, 𝑁 𝑣𝑖 (𝐶𝑈 ), 𝐶𝑉 \ {𝑣 1, ..., 𝑣𝑖 }), where 𝑣𝑖 ∈ 𝐷 and |𝐷 | ≤ |𝑁 𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 )|.

Under the conditions of Theorem 3.2, let 𝑣𝑖 ∈ 𝐷 be a vertex such that |𝑁 𝑣 𝑗 (𝐶𝑈 ) \ 𝑁 𝑣𝑖 (𝐶𝑈 )| = 1 for some 𝑣 𝑗 ∈ 𝐷. Suppose that 𝑢𝑖 is the only vertex in 𝑁 𝑣 𝑗 (𝐶𝑈 )\𝑁 𝑣𝑖 (𝐶𝑈 ). The subinstance 𝐼𝑖 in Theorem 3.2 can be pruned unless 𝑢𝑖 is included the result of 𝐼𝑖 . In Theorem 3.3, checking whether each pair of vertices 𝑣𝑖 and 𝑣 𝑗 in 𝐷 satisfies |𝑁 𝑣 𝑗 (𝐶𝑈 ) \ 𝑁 𝑣𝑖 (𝐶𝑈 )| = 1 incurs significant computational cost. To alleviate this overhead, we employ an approximate strategy that slightly compromises pruning strength in exchange for improved efficiency. Proc. ACM Manag. Our experimental results (see Exp-3) confirm the practical effectiveness of this approximation. The following example illustrates the application of Theorem 3.3. Example 1. Given an instance 𝐼 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ), assume 𝐷 1 = {𝑢 ∈ 𝐶𝑈 |𝑑 𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 ) = 0} and 𝐷 2 = {𝑣 ∈ 𝐶𝑉 |𝑑 𝑣 (𝐶𝑈 ) = 0}. The maximum biclique in 𝐼 must include the vertices in 𝐷 1 and 𝐷 2 . Reduction for special bipartite graphs with max𝑢 ∈𝑈 𝑑 𝑢 (𝐺) ≤ 1 and max𝑣 ∈𝑉 𝑑 𝑣 (𝐺) ≤ 1. Let 𝜔 be the size of the maximum biclique of 𝐺. We observe that 𝜔 can be computed in polynomial time in such case. The following theorem formalizes this result.

Given a bipartite graph 𝐺 = (𝑈 , 𝑉 , 𝐸) where each vertex 𝑢 ∈ 𝑈 (and 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 ) has at least |𝑉 | − 1 (and |𝑈 | − 1) neighbors, let 𝑥 = |𝑈 | × |𝑉 | − |𝐸|, 𝑦 = ||𝑈 | − |𝑉 ||, and 𝑧 = min(|𝑈 |, |𝑉 |). Then, the maximum biclique size 𝜔 in 𝐺 is given by: (1) if 𝑦 ≥ 𝑥, 𝜔 = 𝑧 × (𝑧 + 𝑦 − 𝑥); (2) otherwise, 𝜔 = (𝑧 − ⌊(𝑥 − 𝑦)/2⌋) × (𝑧 − ⌈(𝑥 − 𝑦)/2⌉).

Given a branch 𝐼 = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ), let 𝑢 ∈ 𝐶𝑈 and 𝑣 ∈ 𝐶𝑉 be the two vertices satisfying (𝑢, 𝑣) ∉ 𝐸, 𝑑 𝑢 (𝐶𝑉 ) ≤ 1, and 𝑑 𝑣 (𝐶𝑈 ) ≤ 1. The maximum biclique in 𝐼 is contained within the subinstance 𝐼 ′ = (𝐺, 𝑆𝑈 ∪ {𝑢}, 𝑆𝑉 ∪ {𝑣 }, 𝐶𝑈 \ {𝑢}, 𝐶𝑉 \ {𝑣 }). 3.3 Upper Bound Techniques Except for the basic bounds in [30], we introduce novel upper bounds to eliminate branches that cannot exceed the current maximum biclique size 𝜔. Our approach is based on a sequence ordered by vertex degree, which is displayed in the following lemma.

Following Lemma 3 and earlier discussions, Lemma 4 holds directly, thus we omit its proof. The upper bound-based algorithm. We develop an algorithm that computes the upper bound of Lemma 4, as outlined in Algorithm 1. The algorithm begins by ordering the vertices of 𝑈 and 𝑉 in non-descending order of their degrees (lines 1–2). It then iterates over the vertices in 𝑈 to determine the upper bound 𝜔𝑢𝑏 (lines 3–12), initializing necessary variables for each iteration (lines 3). Given a bipartite graph 𝐺 = (𝑈 , 𝑉 , 𝐸), a pair of subsets (𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ), where 𝑆𝑈 ⊆ 𝑈 and 𝑆𝑉 ⊆ 𝑉 , is a vertex cover of 𝐺 if every edge (𝑢, 𝑣) ∈ 𝐸 satisfies 𝑢 ∈ 𝑆𝑈 or 𝑣 ∈ 𝑆𝑉 . The pair (𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ) is called a minimum vertex cover of 𝐺 if |𝑆𝑈 ∪ 𝑆𝑉 | is minimized over all such covers. For comparison, in a general (non-bipartite) graph 𝐺 = (𝑉 , 𝐸), a vertex cover is a subset 𝐶 ⊆ 𝑉 such that every edge has at least one endpoint in 𝐶. Prior work [41] establishes a tight relationship between the maximum clique and the minimum vertex cover in general graphs, as summarized below. Proc. ACM Manag. [41] Given an arbitrary general (non-bipartite) graph 𝐺 = (𝑉 , 𝐸), let 𝐶 be a minimum vertex cover in the complement graph 𝐺. Then, 𝐺 (𝑉 \ 𝐶) forms a maximum clique in 𝐺. However, we observe that Lemma 5 does not hold when extended to the bipartite graphs. Specifically, consider the complement graph 𝐺 shown in Figure 2. The subgraph 𝐺 ({𝑢 1, 𝑢 4, 𝑢 5 }, {𝑣 4, . . . , 𝑣 20 }), which contains 51 = 3 × 17 edges, is the maximum biclique of the original bipartite graph 𝐺. However, the pair (𝑆𝑈 = {𝑢 1, 𝑢 2, 𝑢 3 }, 𝑆𝑉 = ∅) is the minimum vertex cover of 𝐺, which cannot generate the maximum biclique in 𝐺 by Lemma 5. Furthermore, this discrepancy persists when considering the problem of finding a maximum biclique subject to size constraints. These results indicate that Lemma 5 does not generalize to bipartite graphs. Therefore, it is necessary to establish new structural relationships between bicliques in 𝐺 and vertex covers in its complement 𝐺. Novel duality relationships. Given a vertex cover (𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ) of the complement 𝐺, we say that (𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ) is a minimal vertex cover if it covers all edges of 𝐺, and there exist no proper subsets 𝑆𝑈′ ⊆ 𝑆𝑈 and 𝑆𝑉′ ⊆ 𝑆𝑉 such that (𝑆𝑈′ , 𝑆𝑉′ ) also forms a vertex cover of 𝐺. We now can establish a novel relationship between maximal bicliques in 𝐺 and minimal vertex covers in 𝐺.

Given a bipartite graph 𝐺 = (𝑈 , 𝑉 , 𝐸), let 𝐺 (𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ) be a maximal biclique in 𝐺 such that |𝑆𝑈 | ≥ 𝜏𝑈 and |𝑆𝑉 | ≥ 𝜏𝑉 . Then, (𝑈 \ 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑉 \ 𝑆𝑉 ) forms a minimal vertex cover of 𝐺. Based on Lemma 6, we derive a symmetric result: let (𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ) be a minimal vertex cover of 𝐺 such that |𝑆𝑈 | ≤ |𝑈 | − 𝜏𝑈 and |𝑆𝑉 | ≤ |𝑉 | − 𝜏𝑉 . Then, 𝐺 (𝑈 \ 𝑆𝑈 , 𝑉 \ 𝑆𝑉 ) constitutes the maximal biclique of 𝐺 with |𝑈 \ 𝑆𝑈 | ≥ 𝜏𝑈 and |𝑉 \ 𝑆𝑉 | ≥ 𝜏𝑉 . This observation leads to the following duality theorem, which reformulates the maximum biclique search problem.

Given a bipartite graph 𝐺 = (𝑈 , 𝑉 , 𝐸), the problem of finding the maximum edge biclique in 𝐺 such that each side has cardinality no less than 𝜏𝑈 and 𝜏𝑉 is equivalent to the problem of finding a minimal vertex cover (𝑆𝑈 , 𝑆𝑉 ) of 𝐺 such that |𝑈 \ 𝑆𝑈 | × |𝑉 \ 𝑆𝑉 | is maximized, subject to the constraints |𝑆𝑈 | ≤ 𝛼𝑈 and |𝑆𝑉 | ≤ 𝛼𝑉 , where 𝛼𝑈 + 𝜏𝑈 = |𝑈 |, 𝛼𝑉 + 𝜏𝑉 = |𝑉 |, and 𝜏𝑈 > 0, 𝜏𝑉 > 0. It is important to note that the solutions developed in Sec. 3 cannot be used to solve the problem of minimal vertex cover on 𝐺, since the minimal vertex cover and the maximum biclique are two distinct concepts based on their definitions. Moreover, it is easy to verify that Theorems 3.1-3.3 no longer apply to minimal vertex cover on 𝐺, and therefore the algorithms proposed based on these theorems clearly cannot solve the minimal vertex cover search problem. To address this new problem, we will develop several new techniques in subsequent sections. 4.2 Cover-based Branching Rules Let 𝐵 = (𝐺, 𝑅𝑈 , 𝑅𝑉 , 𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ) denote an instance for computing the minimal vertex covers of 𝐺, where 𝑅𝑈 and 𝑅𝑉 represent the partial vertex cover of 𝐺 (i.e., the minimal vertex cover to be found must include 𝑅𝑈 and 𝑅𝑉 ), 𝐶𝑈 and 𝐶𝑉 induce a subgraph 𝐺 (𝐶𝑈 , 𝐶𝑉 ) to cover. The problem can be addressed via a branch-and-bound framework that leverages a key property: any minimal vertex cover of 𝐺 must either include a given vertex 𝑢 or all of its neighbors in 𝐺. These characteristics offer advantages that extend beyond performance metrics; they provide a principled foundation for algorithm selection, allowing practitioners to reliably choose methods suited for diverse applications.
